subject: What Changed to Your Credit Card Today? Edition 5
summary: RBL Bank quietly dropped the Mastercard option across all three Shoppers Stop card tiers, Gold, Platinum, and Black, issuing on Visa only from now on.
body_html:
What Changed to Your Credit Card Today?

Edition 5, 26 August 2026

If you're the kind of person who signed up for a card years ago and picked the network almost at random, Visa or Mastercard, whichever the branch executive pushed that day, today's change might not feel like it touches you at all. And for most people reading this, it genuinely won't. But RBL Bank just quietly closed off a choice for anyone applying fresh to its Shoppers Stop co-branded lineup: all three tiers, Gold, Platinum, and Black, dropped Mastercard and now issue on Visa only. No press release, no email to existing cardholders, just one line flipped on three product pages the same day. That's small as changes go. It's still worth thirty seconds of your attention if you hold one of these cards, because the "what does this actually mean for me" answer isn't as simple as "nothing."

RBL Bank Shoppers Stop Black Credit Card

This is the top tier of the lineup, ₹10,000 plus GST a year, so roughly ₹11,800 out of your account annually if you're the one paying it, which tells you RBL expects a fairly heavy spender to hold this one. Until this update, you could apply for it on either Visa or Mastercard. Now the product page lists Visa only.

If you already hold the Mastercard version, nothing changes on your card today. It keeps working exactly as it did yesterday, right up to its expiry or your next renewal, at which point RBL will most likely reissue you on Visa instead of Mastercard, though the bank hasn't announced that explicitly. If you're applying fresh from here, you simply don't get asked which network you want anymore.

The catch worth naming honestly: this line change tells you a network disappeared, it doesn't tell you whether anything you actually use disappeared with it. Visa and Mastercard are both accepted almost everywhere in India and abroad today, and RBL sets its own forex markup, typically around 3.5%, regardless of which network sits on the card, so day to day spending shouldn't feel any different. What can change is access to network-specific deals, Mastercard's own dining and movie-ticket tie-ups being the usual example, and those only ever applied if you'd actually enrolled in them. If you never touched those offers, this change costs you nothing. If you did, check your RBL Bank app or Mastercard's own offers page directly rather than assuming you're still covered.

RBL Bank Shoppers Stop Platinum Credit Card

Same call, one tier down: ₹5,000 plus GST a year, and the same Mastercard-to-Visa-only switch landed on this card's page the same day as the Black card above. The mechanics are identical to what I just walked through, so I won't repeat the whole thing. Existing Mastercard cardholders keep their card as is until renewal; new applicants get Visa by default now.

What's actually worth checking on this specific card: banks occasionally run network-exclusive contactless or no-cost EMI tie-ups with select retail partners, and if you've been relying on one of those at a Shoppers Stop store or elsewhere, it's the kind of perk that can quietly stop working once your card gets reissued on a different network, sometimes without the bank flagging it to you directly. I can't tell you from this page change alone whether you personally lose anything; only your own usage can. The check is a two-minute one: open your RBL app, look at which offers are attached to your card today, and note which ones say "Mastercard" specifically.

RBL Bank Shoppers Stop Gold Credit Card

The entry card in the lineup, ₹1,000 plus GST a year, and the tier most people reading this are actually likely to hold given it's the accessible one. Same switch, same day: Mastercard is gone from the application page, Visa only from here.

At this fee level, I'd be surprised if the network switch changes much for most cardholders. This card's appeal was never really about network-specific privileges to begin with; it's about the low entry fee and whatever Shoppers Stop retail benefits come bundled with the co-brand. Acceptance stays universal either way, at Indian merchants and abroad. If there's a catch at all here, it's a smaller one: if you were specifically counting on a Mastercard-network card for reasons of your own, a rewards program tied to Mastercard elsewhere, a family member's card ecosystem, whatever it is, you no longer get that choice on this particular card. Call it a narrowing of options, not a cut to a benefit you're currently using.

What I'd actually do with this

If you already hold any of these three cards, do nothing today. Your card works exactly as it did before this change, and it will keep working until RBL reissues it, most likely at your next renewal cycle. The one thing worth five minutes of your time: open your RBL Bank app and check whether any offer you regularly use is tagged specifically to Mastercard. If none are, this change is genuinely a non-event for you.

If you're applying for one of these cards fresh, you don't have a network decision to make anymore; Visa is what you'll get, and that's fine. Visa's acceptance in India and internationally is every bit as good as Mastercard's for ordinary spending. Pick the card based on the fee and the Shoppers Stop benefits you'll actually use, not the logo on the front.

The fine print

This is my honest read, not formal financial advice. I'm not your advisor, and before you act on anything tied to your own card, especially a network change like this one, check your RBL Bank app and the card's current terms and conditions page directly. But here's exactly how I'd think about it.

Monzy
